newsitem.title: CANADA: Bombardier begins repairs of CRJ cracks.
newsitem.headline: Bombardier begins repairs of CRJ cracks.

text.p: Bombardier Inc said on Friday that repairs had begun on cracks discovered in pressure bulkhead frames on some of the 166 50-seat Canadair Regional Jets (CRJ) delivered to customers.
"We had people already on the spot as of this morning," Catherine Chase, spokeswoman for Bombardier's Canadair unit, told Reuters.
Chase said 102 of the 166 CRJ's had been inspected by Friday morning for possible fatigue cracks in the pressure bulkhead frame at the forward end of the their fuselage wing box cutout.
The inspections were ordered by Transport Canada in an emergency airworthiness directive that became effective on Thursday. Transport Canada issued the directive late on Wednesday.

On June 19, a fatigue crack about 14 inches (35.6 cm) long was discovered in the pressure bulkhead frame of a CRJ owned by U.S. airline SkyWest Inc. The discovery was made after a cabin pressure leak was reported during a flight. The plane landed without incident.
"Inspection of an additional 10 aircraft revealed cracking in the same location on seven," the directive said.
Chase said similar cracks were found on two of the 26 CRJs owned by Air Canada. Two other airlines, one in Europe and one in the United States, also reported cracks in some of their CRJs, she said.

Air Canada spokeswoman Priscille LeBlanc said three of its CRJ round trip flights were canceled on Thursday, but the carrier's schedule returned to normal by Friday. She said all Air Canada's CRJs were being inspected and any repairs would be completed as quickly as possible.
Bombardier shares fell by 1.15 in Toronto late in Thursday's session after market rumors about the canceled Air Canada flights.

"What took place yesterday afternoon was these brokers passing around rumors that there was something wrong with the CRJ, without having any details," said Jon Reider, analyst at RBC Dominion Securities.
Canadair's chief engineer held a telephone conference call with securities firm analysts late on Thursday to discuss the Transport Canada directive, but did not issue a news release on the matter.
"There is no room for interpretation of this as being a more major problem," Reider said.
Bombardier class B shares were up 0.40 to 30.25 in Toronto today on almost 900,000 shares.

Chase said the cracks require minor repairs costing about C$6,000 for each jet. The cracks are located in the pressure bulkhead frame area in front of the jet's wing. The affected area was not part of the wing structure or carry any significant loading, she said.

"Even if this area totally failed, the structural integrity would be maintained, even under ultimate loads," she said. "The only consequence of this cracking is the potential to cause minor pressurization leaks."
Chase said Canadair had assembled 75 repair kits, which included sheet metal and fasteners that would be used to reinforce the problem area.
"Any aircraft leaving the factory now will have a permanent fix in it," she said.
